context: linear & networked · trenching production rate, crossings & live tie-in govern the programme

brief.intro: New to this project type? A utilities distribution network project lays buried pipes and cables — water, power, gas or telecom — along a route or across a site or municipality, rather than building a single structure. Progress is measured along the alignment by chainage, not by floors or rooms, and the real driver of the programme is production rate: metres of trench excavated, pipe or cable laid, and backfilled per day, repeated the whole way along. The trickiest part isn't the open trench itself — it's crossing existing roads, rail lines, rivers or other buried utilities, and the final live tie-in and switchover into the operating network, which is usually a short, tightly permitted window that cannot simply be rescheduled.

scope.name: Route survey, utility mapping & permits
scope.desc: Locating existing buried services and obtaining way-leaves and road-opening permits before any digging.

scope.name: Trenching & excavation
scope.desc: Open-cut excavation along the alignment, or trenchless methods where open-cut isn't possible.

scope.name: Pipe / cable laying
scope.desc: Bedding, laying and jointing the pipe or cable to specification.

scope.name: Crossings & special works
scope.desc: Road, rail and river crossings by thrust-bore, directional drill or slab, where the route can't be open-cut.

scope.name: Chambers & appurtenances
scope.desc: Valve chambers, manholes, draw-pits and meter pits built along the route.

scope.name: Backfill & reinstatement
scope.desc: Compaction and surface reinstatement to match the original road, footpath or landscaping.

scope.name: Earthing & cathodic protection
scope.desc: Bonding along the route and, for steel pipelines, corrosion protection systems.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: Pressure and disinfection testing for pipe, or HV/LV testing and energisation for cable.

scope.name: SCADA / telemetry & metering
scope.desc: Instrumentation that lets the network operator monitor and control the new network remotely.

scope.name: Live tie-ins & switchover
scope.desc: Physically connecting the new network into the existing, operating network — the highest-risk step in the programme.

must_get_right: Production rate (metres per day of trench, lay and backfill) is the schedule engine — plan and track it like a production line, chainage by chainage.
Crossings (road, rail, river) and interfaces with other buried utilities are the real schedule risk — locate and sequence them early, not as an afterthought.
Protect a real, permitted window for the live tie-in and switchover — it is often the only time supply can be interrupted, and re-scheduling it costs weeks.
Road-opening and way-leave permits sit on the critical path just as much as the physical work — track them as milestones, not admin.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by route chainage so production progress (metres trenched, laid, tested) is visible section by section, not just as a task list.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Trenching and laying run extended daytime hours; traffic-management restrictions may limit night or weekend working in public roads. Live tie-ins and switchovers are typically scheduled as an isolated night or weekend shutdown window agreed in advance with the network operator, on its own calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path repeats chainage by chainage: permits/way-leaves → trench → lay/joint → test → tie-in/switchover. Crossings (road, rail, river) and interfaces with existing utilities are the schedule-critical pinch points along the route, and the final live tie-in is typically the last and most constrained activity in the whole programme.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The route is free of undisclosed utility clashes beyond what the survey found; permits and way-leaves are granted on the assumed programme; a single mobilisation; and the network operator provides the tie-in/shutdown window on the date assumed.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive sections of the network:

rows: Before the pipe-laying front reaches that section

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Work in live streets requires traffic management and road-opening permits, and crews must operate near existing, often undocumented, services. Trenching plant and crews are the production-rate resource and are sized to the target metres-per-day; crossings are further constrained by rail possessions or river low-flow seasons.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: undisclosed existing services causing clashes or damage, permit delays, adverse ground conditions (rock, high water table), and tie-in window slippage. Schedule contingency is held around crossings and immediately before the live tie-in/switchover, rather than spread thinly across the route.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by route section; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for trenching crews — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
